nameStory: This moth was recently renamed from "gypsy moth" to "spongy moth" because the former name was considered a slur against the Romani people. The new name "spongy" refers to the distinctive texture of the female's egg masses, which feel soft and foamy to the touch, like a natural sponge.
description: The spongy moth is a medium-sized moth originally from Europe and Asia that has become one of New England's most notorious invasive insects. Adult males are brownish with feathery antennae and can fly, while females are larger, whitish, and flightless with simple antennae. The caterpillars are the real troublemakers - hairy, colorful larvae that can completely strip leaves from entire forests during outbreak years.

idTips.label: Male vs Female Differences
idTips.description: Males are smaller, brown, and flutter around lights, while females are much larger, cream-colored with black markings, and cannot fly at all - you'll find them sitting motionless on tree trunks

idTips.label: Caterpillar Appearance
idTips.description: Larvae have a distinctive pattern of blue and red dots along their backs - five pairs of blue dots followed by six pairs of red dots - and are covered in long, irritating hairs

idTips.label: Egg Mass Texture
idTips.description: Tan-colored egg masses feel spongy and soft when fresh, like touching a foam pad, and are covered with buff-colored hairs from the female's body

idTips.label: Male Antennae
idTips.description: Males have distinctly feathery, branched antennae that look like tiny ferns, much more elaborate than most other moths

idTips.label: Defoliation Pattern
idTips.description: Look for trees that are completely stripped of leaves in mid-summer, often starting at the top and working down, with dark droppings covering the ground below

habitat: Found throughout New England's deciduous and mixed forests, particularly favoring oak, birch, and aspen trees. During outbreak years, you'll encounter them virtually everywhere - from backyard shade trees to deep wilderness areas. They thrive in disturbed forest edges and suburban areas where their preferred host trees are abundant.

seasonality.spring: Tiny caterpillars emerge from overwintering egg masses in May, initially staying high in tree crowns where they're hard to spot but leave small holes in new leaves.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity time - large caterpillars are everywhere, defoliating trees and pupating in July, while adults emerge and mate in late July through August.
seasonality.fall: Females lay distinctive spongy egg masses on tree trunks, rocks, and outdoor furniture - this is the easiest time to spot evidence of their presence.
seasonality.winter: Only egg masses are visible, appearing as tan, oval patches on bark that remain soft to the touch even in cold weather.

funFact: A single spongy moth caterpillar can eat an entire square foot of leaves per day during its final growth stage, and one outbreak can consume more forest vegetation than all the deer, moose, and other herbivores in New England combined!
confusionNotes: The hairy caterpillars might be confused with other fuzzy species like woolly bears, but spongy moth larvae are the only ones with that distinctive blue-dot-then-red-dot pattern down their backs. Remember: "Blue before red, cause for dread."
contextualKnowledge: The name change from "gypsy moth" to "spongy moth" happened in 2022 as part of an effort by entomologists to remove offensive terms from scientific naming. You'll still see the old name in older field guides and online resources, but both names refer to the same species.
compareHints: Since this is the only Lymantria species established in New England, compare it to other tussock moths in the same family. Unlike native tussock moths, spongy moth females are much larger and completely flightless, and their caterpillars lack the distinctive hair tufts that give tussock moths their name.

ecologicalRole.pestNote: Major forest defoliator — caterpillars strip hardwood trees
